# Pulmonary embolism

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Pulmonology > Pulmonary vascular disorders > Pulmonary embolism*

[Original Article Link](/library/oh00Uf)

---

## Summary

Pulmonary embolism (<u>PE</u>) is the obstruction of one or more <u>pulmonary arteries</u> by an embolic solid, fluid, or gas. In the majority of cases, <u>PE</u> is caused by a <u>venous thrombus</u> that originated in the legs or <u>pelvis</u> and embolized to the <u>lungs</u> via the <u>inferior vena cava</u>. <u>Risk factors</u> include immobility, inherited <u>hypercoagulability</u> disorders, <u>pregnancy</u>, <u>postpartum period</u>, and recent <u>surgery</u>. The clinical presentation can range from asymptomatic to <u>obstructive shock</u>, depending on the extent of <u>pulmonary artery</u> obstruction. Because symptoms are often nonspecific (e.g., <u>chest pain</u>, <u>coughing</u>, <u>shortness of breath</u>, and <u>tachycardia</u>), <u>PE</u> should be considered in all patients with acute <u>dyspnea</u>. A tentative diagnosis of <u>PE</u> is usually based on history and clinical suspicion, then confirmed with <u>CT pulmonary angiography</u> (<u>CTPA</u>). <u>Arterial blood gas analysis</u> (<u>ABG</u>) may be normal or show low partial oxygen pressure and <u>respiratory alkalosis</u>. Serum <u>D-dimer</u> test is highly sensitive for <u>PE</u> and can help rule out the diagnosis. Therapeutic anticoagulation is initiated to prevent further embolic events and to promote the gradual dissolution of the embolism and any underlying <u>thrombosis</u>. Treatment for <u>massive PE</u> with <u>hemodynamic instability</u> additionally involves restoring pulmonary <u>perfusion</u> with thrombolytic agents and/or embolectomy.




See also “<u>Nonthrombotic embolism</u>” and “<u>Deep vein thrombosis</u>.”

---

## Etiology

* Most common: : <u>Deep vein thrombosis</u> (See “<u>Risk factors for VTE</u>.”) [[2]](/library/J1Xs3C)

* Causes of <u>nonthrombotic embolism</u>

* <u>Fat embolism</u>

* <u>Air embolism</u>

* <u>Amniotic fluid embolism</u>

* Others: <u>bacterial embolism</u>, <u>pulmonary tumor embolism</u>, <u>pulmonary cement embolism</u>





> [!NOTE]
> <u>PE</u> is FATAL: <u>PE</u> caused by Fat, Air, Thrombus, Amniotic fluid, and Less common, i.e., bacterial, <u>tumor</u>, and cement.

---

## Pathophysiology

* Mechanism: <u>thrombus formation</u> (see “<u>Virchow's triad</u>.”) → <u>deep vein thrombosis</u> in the legs or <u>pelvis</u> (most commonly iliac <u>vein</u>) → embolization to <u>pulmonary arteries</u> via <u>inferior vena cava</u>;   → partial or complete obstruction of <u>pulmonary arteries</u>   [[2]](/library/J1Xs3C)

* Pathophysiologic response of the <u>lung</u> to arterial obstruction ;   [[2]](/library/J1Xs3C)

* <u>Infarction</u> and inflammation of the <u>lungs</u> and <u>pleura</u>

* Causes <u>pleuritic chest pain</u> and <u>hemoptysis</u>

* Leads to <u>surfactant</u> dysfunction → <u>atelectasis</u> → ↓ <u>PaO<sub>2</sub></u>  [[3]](/library/I1XYRC)

* Triggers respiratory drive → <u>hyperventilation</u> and <u>tachypnea</u> → <u>respiratory alkalosis</u> with <u>hypocapnia</u> (↓ <u>PaCO<sub>2</sub></u>)

* Impaired <u>gas exchange</u>
* Mechanical vessel obstruction → <u>ventilation-perfusion mismatch</u>  → arterial <u>hypoxemia</u> (↓ <u>PaO<sub>2</sub></u>) and elevated <u>A-a gradient</u>  (See “Diagnostics” below.)

* Cardiac compromise
* Elevated <u>pulmonary artery</u> pressure (<u>PAP</u>) due to blockage → <u>right ventricular</u> pressure overload → forward failure with decreased <u>cardiac output</u>  → <u>hypotension</u> and <u>tachycardia</u>

* Pulmonary <u>vasoconstriction</u>: <u>thromboxane A<sub>2</sub></u>, <u>prostaglandins</u>, <u>adenosine</u>, <u>thrombin</u>, and <u>serotonin</u> secreted by activated <u>platelet</u> and the <u>thrombus</u> → pulmonary <u>vasoconstriction</u> and <u>bronchospasm</u> [[4]](/library/q1XC3C)

* Saddle thrombus  

* A blood clot (e.g., from <u>deep vein thrombosis</u>) that lodges at the bifurcation of the <u>pulmonary trunk</u> as it splits into the right and left <u>pulmonary arteries</u>.

* Can obstruct blood flow through the <u>pulmonary arteries</u> and lead to right <u>heart</u> strain, <u>hemodynamic instability</u>, and/or <u>death</u>.

## Clinical features

* Common <u>features of PE</u> ;  [[5]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

* Acute onset of symptoms

* <u>Dyspnea</u> (> 75% of cases) [[5]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

* <u>Tachycardia</u> and <u>tachypnea</u> (up to 50% of cases) [[5]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

* Sudden <u>pleuritic chest pain</u> (∼ 20% of cases)  [[5]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

* <u>Cough</u> and <u>hemoptysis</u>

* Associated <u>features of DVT</u>: e.g., unilaterally painful leg swelling  [[6]](/library/8I1OeR0)

* Less common <u>features of PE</u> [[5]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

* Decreased breath sounds

* Dullness to percussion

* <u>Split S2</u>

* Low-grade <u>fever</u>

* Rarely, upper abdominal <u>pain</u> [[7]](/library/uI1peR0)[[8]](/library/J-csyU0)

* Features of <u>massive PE</u> (e.g., due to a <u>saddle thrombus</u>)

* <u>Presyncope</u> or <u>syncope</u>

* <u>Jugular venous distension</u>;   and <u>Kussmaul sign</u>

* <u>Hypotension</u> and <u>obstructive shock</u>

* Circulatory collapse

* Features of intraoperative PE: all features typically have an abrupt onset [[9]](/library/71X4RC)[[10]](/library/5P1i2S0)

* Decrease in <u>EtCO<sub>2</sub></u> (early sign)

* Decrease in <u>SpO<sub>2</sub></u>

* <u>Hypotension</u>

* <u>Tachycardia</u>





> [!TIP]
> Most patients with <u>PE</u> have a grossly normal <u>physical examination</u>; abnormalities heard on <u>lung auscultation</u> (e.g., <u>wheezes</u> or bilateral <u>rales</u>) often suggest a different cause for the symptoms. [[5]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




> [!TIP]
> Consider <u>PE</u> as a differential diagnosis in recurring or progressive <u>dyspnea</u> of uncertain etiology.

## Pretest probability of pulmonary embolism

### Overview [[11]](/library/PBYWa7)[[12]](/library/0BYezr)




Estimate <u>pretest probability</u> (<u>PTP</u>) using validated tools and/or <u>clinician gestalt</u> to guide diagnostic testing.  [[11]](/library/PBYWa7)[[12]](/library/0BYezr)[[13]](/library/sCctte0)




* High PTP of PE

* <u>Modified Wells score</u> > 4

* <u>Original Wells score</u> ≥ 7

* <u>Revised Geneva score</u> > 10

* Intermediate PTP of PE

* <u>Original Wells score</u> 2–6

* <u>Revised Geneva score</u> 4–10

* Low PTP of PE

* <u>Modified Wells score</u> ≤ 4

* <u>Original Wells score</u> < 2

* <u>Revised Geneva score</u> < 4

* Very low <u>PTP of PE</u>: <u>Low PTP of PE</u> plus <u>PERC</u> = 0





### Wells criteria for pulmonary embolism [[14]](/library/cBYa-r)




The <u>Wells score</u> is a diagnostic algorithm for assessing the <u>probability</u> of <u>PE</u> and has been validated in inpatient and outpatient settings. Use “<u>Wells criteria for DVT</u>” to calculate the <u>PTP</u> of <u>deep vein thrombosis</u>.




| <br><u>Wells criteria for PE</u> [[15]](/library/V_YGM7)[[16]](/library/n1b7hs)<br> |  |
| --- | --- |
| Criteria | Points |
| Clinical symptoms of <u>DVT</u> | 3 |
| <u>PE</u> more likely than other diagnoses | 3 |
| Previous <u>PE</u>/<u>DVT</u> | 1.5 |
| <br><u>Tachycardia</u> (<u>heart rate</u> > 100/min) | 1.5 |
| <u>Surgery</u> or <u>immobilization</u> in the past 4 weeks | 1.5 |
| <u>Hemoptysis</u> | 1 |
| <br><u>Malignancy</u><br> | 1 |
| <br>Original Wells score (clinical <u>probability</u>) [[15]](/library/V_YGM7) <br><br>* Total score 0–1: low <u>probability</u> of <u>PE</u> (6%)<br><br>* Total score 2–6: intermediate <u>probability</u> of <u>PE</u> (23%)<br><br>* Total score ≥ 7: high <u>probability</u> of <u>PE</u> (49%)<br><br><br><br> |  |
| <br>Modified Wells score (simplified clinical <u>probability</u>) [[16]](/library/n1b7hs) <br><br>* Total score ≤ 4: <u>PE</u> unlikely (8%)<br><br>* Total score > 4: <u>PE</u> likely (34%)<br><br><br><br> |  |





![Wells Criteria for pulmonary embolism](media/maz0jwg04feqx3okzdu159dl.jpg)

Wells Criteria for pulmonary embolism




### Revised Geneva score [[17]](/library/1BY2-r)




The <u>revised Geneva score</u> utilizes objective clinical variables. It has been externally validated and was initially studied in emergency department outpatients.




| <br><u>Revised Geneva score</u> [[15]](/library/V_YGM7)<br> |  |
| --- | --- |
| Criteria | Points |
| Age > 65 years | 1 |
| Prior history of <u>DVT</u> or <u>PE</u> | 3 |
| <br>Recent <u>surgery</u>  or <u>fracture</u> of the lower limbs <br> | 2 |
| <br>Personal history of cancer <br> | 2 |
| Unilateral lower limb <u>pain</u> | 3 |
| <u>Hemoptysis</u> | 2 |
| <u>Heart rate</u> 75–94/min | 3 |
| <u>Heart rate</u> ≥ 95/min | 5 |
| <u>Pain</u> on palpation of lower limb and unilateral <u>edema</u> | 4 |
| <br>Clinical <u>pretest probability</u> <br><br>* Total score < 4: low <u>probability</u> of <u>PE</u> (9%)<br><br>* Total score 4–10: intermediate <u>probability</u> of <u>PE</u> (26%)<br><br>* Total score > 10: high <u>probability</u> of <u>PE</u> (76%)<br><br><br><br> |  |





![Revised Geneva score for pulmonary embolism](media/zp5uzbowiggedx6zk8z6rqul.jpg)

Revised Geneva score for pulmonary embolism




### <u>Pulmonary embolism rule-out criteria</u> (<u>PERC</u>)  [[12]](/library/0BYezr)[[18]](/library/4BY3a7)[[19]](/library/kBYma7)




Patients with a <u>low PTP of PE</u> and a <u>PERC score</u> of zero have a very low <u>probability</u> of <u>PE</u> and require no further testing. [[20]](/library/xsdECr0)




| Pulmonary embolism rule-out criteria (<u>PERC</u>) |  |
| --- | --- |
| Criteria | Points |
| Age > 50 years | 1 |
| <u>Heart rate</u> > 100/min | 1 |
| <br><u>Oxygen saturation</u> < 95% <br> | 1 |
| <u>Hemoptysis</u> | 1 |
| <u>Estrogen</u> use | 1 |
| Prior history of <u>DVT</u> or <u>PE</u> | 1 |
| <br>Recent <u>surgery</u> or trauma  in the past 4 weeks<br> | 1 |
| Unilateral lower limb <u>edema</u> | 1 |
| <br>Clinical <u>pretest probability</u> <br><br>* Total score 0: <u>pretest probability</u> < 1%; no further testing needed<br><br>* Total score ≥ 1: <u>PE</u> is not ruled out; further testing needed<br><br><br><br> |  |





> [!TIP]
> <u>PERC</u> should only be used in patients with a previously determined <u>low PTP of PE</u>.




> [!WARNING]
> The presence of any <u>PERC</u> criteria in a patient with suspected <u>PE</u> necessitates further testing.




![Pulmonary embolism rule-out criteria (PERC)](media/gcnphc2kch2pkyjguwblmuag.jpg)

Pulmonary embolism rule-out criteria (PERC)

## Diagnosis

### Approach [[5]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[12]](/library/0BYezr)[[21]](/library/-xYD_r)




* <u>Hemodynamically unstable</u> patients: Begin <u>management of massive PE</u> prior to diagnostic confirmation.  [[22]](/library/Z_YZ57)

* Assess for signs of RV dysfunction.

* Obtain an <u>ECG</u>.

* Perform a bedside <u>echocardiogram</u> or <u>focused cardiac ultrasound</u> (<u>FoCUS</u>)  [[22]](/library/Z_YZ57)[[23]](/library/jWb_Os)

* Consider adding <u>DVT point-of-care ultrasound</u> (<u>POCUS</u>).  [[24]](/library/FxbgyD)

* Obtain confirmatory imaging (<u>CTPA</u> or <u>V/Q scan</u>) when stable enough for transport.

* Hemodynamically stable patients (e.g., systolic BP > 90 mm Hg): Assess <u>PTP of PE</u>. 

* <u>Low PTP of PE</u>

* <u>PERC</u> = 0: No further testing for <u>PE</u> is required.

* <u>PERC</u> > 0: Obtain <u>D-dimer</u>.

* Elevated <u>D-dimer</u>: Obtain confirmatory imaging.

* Normal <u>D-dimer</u>: No further testing for <u>PE</u> is required; consider alternative diagnoses.

* <u>Intermediate PTP of PE</u>: Obtain <u>D-dimer</u>.

* Elevated <u>D-dimer</u>: Obtain confirmatory imaging.

* Normal <u>D-dimer</u>: No further testing for <u>PE</u> is required; consider alternative diagnoses.

* <u>High PTP of PE</u>: Obtain confirmatory imaging.

* Confirmed <u>PE</u>: Assess severity using <u>ECG</u>, <u>cardiac biomarkers</u>, and imaging (e.g., <u>CTPA</u> or <u>echocardiography</u>) [[22]](/library/Z_YZ57)[[25]](/library/9XXNZC)





![Diagnostic approach to pulmonary embolism](media/j3qbgbdrcq5xfyqnz1o8obhv.jpg)

Diagnostic approach to pulmonary embolism




### Initial evaluation




The initial evaluation of patients with <u>dyspnea</u> and/or <u>chest pain</u> typically includes <u>laboratory studies</u>, <u>CXR</u>, and <u>ECG</u>. Findings may suggest but do not confirm <u>PE</u>. [[5]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




#### <u>D-dimer</u>  [[12]](/library/0BYezr)[[22]](/library/Z_YZ57)




* Indications

* <u>Intermediate PTP of PE</u>

* <u>Low PTP of PE</u> and <u>PERC</u> > 0

* Findings

* Normal levels: < 500 ng/mL

* If â¥ 500 ng/mL: Further testing is required (see below).

* If the patient is > 50 years of age, adjust for age: age x 10 ng/mL = cutoff value in ng/mL  [[12]](/library/0BYezr)[[20]](/library/xsdECr0)[[26]](/library/l1XvSC)

* Interpretation

* High <u>sensitivity</u> and <u>negative predictive value</u>: A negative <u>D-dimer</u> test most likely rules out <u>PE</u>.

* Low <u>specificity</u>: positive results in all forms of <u>fibrinolysis</u>





> [!TIP]
> Normal <u>D-dimer</u> values usually rule out <u>PE</u> or <u>DVT</u> in patients with a low <u>PTP</u>. A positive <u>D-dimer</u> is nonspecific, since it may be elevated in any situation in which there is increased <u>fibrinolysis</u>.




#### Additional <u>laboratory studies</u> [[12]](/library/0BYezr)




* <u>Arterial blood gas</u> (<u>ABG</u>) [[27]](/library/K1bU3s)[[28]](/library/61bj3s)

* Often normal

* Common findings

* ↑ <u>Alveolar-arterial gradient</u>

* <u>Hypoxemia</u> (e.g., ↓ <u>SaO<sub>2</sub></u>, <u>PaO₂</u> < 80 mm Hg)

* <u>Respiratory alkalosis</u>

* <u>CBC</u>: may show <u>leukocytosis</u>  [[29]](/library/md1Vqf0)

* <u>BMP</u>: used to assess renal function

* <u>Cardiac biomarkers</u>: e.g., <u>troponin</u>, <u>BNP</u>, <u>NT-proBNP</u> (See “Severity assessment” for interpretation.)





> [!WARNING]
> A normal <u>oxygen saturation</u> and/or normal <u>PaO<sub>2</sub></u> do not rule out <u>PE</u>. [[5]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[30]](/library/hW1cOf0)




#### <u>Chest x-ray</u>  [[23]](/library/jWb_Os)




* Characteristic findings

* Hampton hump: a wedge-shaped opacity in the peripheral <u>lung</u> with its base at the thoracic wall; caused by <u>pulmonary infarction</u> and not specific for <u>PE</u>

* Westermark sign: an area of <u>lung parenchyma</u> lucency caused by oligemia secondary to occlusion of blood flow

* Fleischner sign: a prominent <u>pulmonary artery</u> caused by vessel distention due to a large pulmonary <u>embolus</u> (common in <u>massive PE</u>)

* Nonspecific findings

* <u>Atelectasis</u>

* <u>Pleural effusions</u>

* <u>Cardiomegaly</u>

Fleischner sign, Westermark sign, and knuckle sign in pulmonary embolism




#### <u>Electrocardiography</u> (<u>ECG</u>)




* Most common findings [[31]](/library/bfbHkG)

* <u>T-wave inversions</u> or flattening

* Sinus <u>tachycardia</u>

* Normal <u>ECG</u>

* Predictors of adverse outcomes: See “<u>High-risk ECG findings in PE</u>.”

* Other <u>ECG</u> findings in <u>PE</u>: <u>sinus bradycardia</u> (< 60/min); uncommon)  [[32]](/library/cdbaKs)





![ECG of a patient with pulmonary embolism](media/vsabunojy4jtrueqq5kgqhtw.jpg)

ECG of a patient with pulmonary embolism




### Confirmatory imaging




#### CT pulmonary angiography (<u>CTPA</u>) [[12]](/library/0BYezr)[[23]](/library/jWb_Os)[[33]](/library/ZBYZzr)




<u>CTPA</u> is the preferred test for the diagnosis of acute <u>PE</u>.  [[23]](/library/jWb_Os)




* Technique: CT chest with bolus IV contrast <u>enhancement</u> of the <u>pulmonary arteries</u>

* Indications

* All patients with a <u>high PTP of PE</u>

* Elevated <u>D-dimer</u> in patients with a low or <u>intermediate PTP of PE</u>

* Contraindications

* <u>Renal insufficiency</u>

* Contrast <u>allergy</u>

* Findings

* Direct finding of <u>PE</u>: intraluminal filling defects of <u>pulmonary arteries</u>

* <u>Pulmonary infarct</u>: opacity with consolidated border; may be accompanied by <u>pleural effusion</u>

* Evidence of RV dysfunction  [[34]](/library/JV1svf0)





> [!NOTE]
> A wedge-shaped <u>infarction</u> with <u>pleural effusion</u> is almost <u>pathognomonic</u> for <u>PE</u>. [[23]](/library/jWb_Os)

#### Ventilation/perfusion scintigraphy (<u>V/Q scan</u>)  [[12]](/library/0BYezr)[[23]](/library/jWb_Os)




* Technique: comparison of <u>perfusion and ventilation scintigraphy</u> to identify <u>ventilation-perfusion mismatch</u>

* Indication: alternative to <u>CTPA</u> in patients with <u>contraindications for iodinated IV contrast</u>

* Findings [[33]](/library/ZBYZzr)[[35]](/library/dyYoV7)

* The absence of <u>perfusion</u> in normally ventilated areas of the <u>lung</u> (mismatch) suggests <u>PE</u>.

* Discordance between <u>V/Q scan</u> results and the clinical <u>PTP</u> necessitates further evaluation.





> [!TIP]
> <u>CTPA</u> and <u>V/Q scans</u> have similar <u>sensitivities</u> and specificities for <u>PE</u>, but <u>CTPA</u> is faster and more readily available. [[23]](/library/jWb_Os)




![Mismatched perfusion defects from pulmonary emboli](media/s2o0w0bcr277dpy2wvpo20m0.jpg)

Mismatched perfusion defects from pulmonary emboli




#### Pulmonary angiography [[23]](/library/jWb_Os)[[33]](/library/ZBYZzr)




* Technique: selective injection of contrast dye into the <u>pulmonary arteries</u> during <u>fluoroscopic</u> examination

* Indications

* Inconclusive <u>CTPA</u> findings and high level of suspicion for <u>PE</u>

* Candidates for concomitant endovascular treatment, e.g., embolectomy

* Findings: intraluminal filling defects in <u>pulmonary arteries</u>





![Pulmonary angiography](media/k00kgoopmzv6ksr7mh5vtabn.jpg)

Pulmonary angiography




### Adjunctive imaging




* <u>Lower extremity venous ultrasound</u> [[12]](/library/0BYezr)[[21]](/library/-xYD_r)

* Indications

* Symptoms of <u>deep venous thrombosis</u>  and pulmonary embolism

* Contraindications to <u>CTPA</u> (e.g., contrast <u>allergy</u> and <u>renal insufficiency</u>)

* <u>Pregnancy</u>

* Findings: e.g., noncompressible <u>deep vein</u> (See “<u>Ultrasound findings of DVT</u>” for details. 

* High <u>sensitivity</u> for <u>DVT</u> but not for <u>PE</u>

* A negative <u>ultrasound</u> does not rule out <u>PE</u>. [[36]](/library/edbxKs)[[37]](/library/Udbb6s)

* POCUS in VTE  [[38]](/library/0V1eGf0)[[39]](/library/dV1otf0)[[40]](/library/VV1Gtf0)

* Clinical applications

* Supporting a <u>clinical diagnosis</u> of <u>VTE</u> in patients who cannot undergo prompt confirmatory imaging

* Evaluating for alternative diagnoses

* Techniques: See “<u>Focused cardiac ultrasound</u> (<u>FoCUS</u>),” “<u>POCUS for DVT</u>” and “<u>Lung POCUS</u>.”

* Findings

* <u>FoCUS</u>: Signs of RV strain (e.g., <u>D-sign</u>, RV enlargement) may be present.

* <u>POCUS for DVT</u>: Signs of an incompressible <u>proximal</u> <u>deep vein</u> may be present.

* <u>Lung POCUS</u>: Signs of alternative diagnoses (e.g., <u>pneumonia</u>, <u>pulmonary edema</u>) may be present.

* Magnetic resonance <u>pulmonary angiography</u>: if <u>CTPA</u> or <u>V/Q scan</u> cannot be performed  [[23]](/library/jWb_Os)[[41]](/library/eyYxV7)





> [!TIP]
> The absence of a <u>DVT</u> does not rule out <u>PE</u>, but the presence of a <u>DVT</u> can justify starting <u>empiric anticoagulation for PE</u>. [[38]](/library/0V1eGf0)




![POCUS protocol for detection of lower extremity DVT](media/ibhxrbtm6tkih2tuu4cauvm1.jpg)

POCUS protocol for detection of lower extremity DVT




### Severity assessment [[22]](/library/Z_YZ57)[[42]](/library/VyYGV7)[[43]](/library/8d1O7f0)




Signs of RV dysfunction that predict adverse outcomes (e.g., hemodynamic collapse or <u>death</u>) can be identified clinically, electrically, biochemically, and radiologically (e.g., on <u>echocardiography</u> or <u>CTPA</u>). [[22]](/library/Z_YZ57)[[25]](/library/9XXNZC)[[43]](/library/8d1O7f0)




#### <u>ECG</u> and <u>cardiac biomarkers</u>




* High-risk ECG findings in PE [[44]](/library/Ydbnos)[[45]](/library/adbQos)

* Signs of right <u>heart</u> strain [[5]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

* <u>S<sub>I</sub>Q<sub>III</sub>T<sub>III</sub>-pattern</u>

* New <u>right bundle branch block</u> (incomplete or complete)

* <u>T-wave inversion</u> in <u>anterior</u> <u>precordial leads</u> (V<sub>1</sub>–V<sub>4</sub>)

* <u>Sinus tachycardia</u> (> 100/min)

* <u>Atrial fibrillation</u>

* <u>ST elevation</u> in aVR

* <u>Q waves</u> in III and <u>aVF</u>

* <u>Troponin</u>: elevated if <u>myocardial</u> damage has occurred  [[22]](/library/Z_YZ57)[[46]](/library/JBYsb7)

* <u>B-type natriuretic peptide</u> (<u>BNP</u>) or <u>NT-proBNP</u>: identifies RV strain  [[22]](/library/Z_YZ57)[[47]](/library/IBYYX7)





> [!TIP]
> ↑ <u>BNP</u> is nonspecific but can predict early adverse outcomes in patients with <u>PE</u>. [[22]](/library/Z_YZ57)




#### <u>Echocardiography</u>




* Goal: mostly used for prognosis; can be used as a diagnostic tool in patients too unstable for confirmatory imaging

* Indications

* Suspected right-<u>heart</u> strain or RV dysfunction

* Critically ill patients with suspected <u>PE</u>

* Findings  [[22]](/library/Z_YZ57)[[23]](/library/jWb_Os)[[43]](/library/8d1O7f0)

* Dilatation and hypokinesis of the <u>right ventricle</u> (RV)

* RV dysfunction

* McConnell sign: <u>akinesia</u> of the mid-free RV wall and hypercontractility of the apical wall

* Venous reflux with <u>IVC</u> dilation

* <u>Tricuspid regurgitation</u> (<u>tricuspid valve</u> insufficiency)

* ↑ <u>PASP</u>

* Increased <u>right atrial pressure</u>





> [!TIP]
> The presence or absence of RV dysfunction guides the risk <u>stratification</u> and subsequent management of hemodynamically stable patients with <u>PE</u>. [[25]](/library/9XXNZC)[[48]](/library/qV1Cvf0)




![Dilated right heart with right ventricular strain](media/hn6egd9yxdgwk9i23y393bbq.jpg)

Dilated right heart with right ventricular strain




### Identification of underlying pathology




* Evaluation for <u>thrombophilia</u> [[49]](/library/UyYbe7)

* Indicated in younger patients with any of the following

* No or weak <u>risk factors</u>

* <u>Family history</u>

* Recurrence of venous <u>thrombosis</u>

* Timing: after the completion of therapy

* See “<u>Hypercoagulable states</u>.”

* Evaluation for malignancies: age-appropriate <u>screening studies</u>; See “Preventive Medicine.”

---

## Pathology

* Purpose: distinguishing cause of embolism (See “Etiology”.)

* Histological findings [[50]](/library/r1XfRC)

* Lines of Zahn: alternating layers of <u>platelets</u> mixed with <u>fibrin</u> (light pink layers) and <u>red blood cells</u> (dark red layers)

* Only appear premortally (help distinguish a premortal <u>thrombus</u> from a postmortem one)





![Lines of Zahn](media/yvom3sfa5ooj2dq1d7gs9ur3.jpg)

Lines of Zahn

---

## Differential diagnoses

* See “<u>Differential diagnosis of chest pain</u>.”

* See “<u>Differential diagnosis of dyspnea</u>.”

* Other causes of <u>obstructive shock</u>, e.g., <u>cardiac tamponade</u>, <u>tension pneumothorax</u>

* <u>Postoperative atelectasis</u>

* <u>Anxiety disorders</u>




The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

---

## Management

### General principles [[22]](/library/Z_YZ57)[[48]](/library/qV1Cvf0)[[54]](/library/q11C3f0)




* Manage unstable patients using the <u>ABCDE approach</u> (see “<u>Management of massive PE</u>”).

* Provide <u>oxygen therapy</u> for <u>hypoxic</u> patients.

* <u>Treat PE based on severity</u> and bleeding risk; start <u>empiric anticoagulation for PE</u> if indicated.

* Provide <u>analgesia</u>; avoid <u>NSAIDs</u> if possible.

* Consult a pulmonary embolism response team (<u>PERT</u>), if available: A multidisciplinary team that coordinates the management of patients with <u>PE</u>  [[48]](/library/qV1Cvf0)[[55]](/library/-AYDm7)

* Consider calculating <u>PESI</u> or <u>sPESI score</u> to guide disposition.





> [!WARNING]
> Start <u>empiric anticoagulation for PE</u> if clinical suspicion is high unless there is a high risk of bleeding (e.g., recent <u>surgery</u>, <u>hemorrhagic stroke</u>, active bleeding). [[48]](/library/qV1Cvf0)




### Overview of treatment options by severity




| <br>Pulmonary embolism treatment by severity and bleeding risk [[25]](/library/9XXNZC)[[48]](/library/qV1Cvf0)[[54]](/library/q11C3f0)<br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | Bleeding risk |  |
| Low | <br>High<br> |  |
| <u>Nonmassive PE</u> | <br><br>* <u>Anticoagulation for PE</u> in most patients<br><br>* Consider <u>conservative management</u> only for patients with subsegmental <u>PE</u>, no <u>proximal DVT</u>, and a low risk of recurrence<br><br>* Outpatient management is often appropriate.<br><br><br> | <br>* Consider a temporary <u>IVC filter</u>.<br><br> |
| <u>Submassive PE</u> | <br><br>* <u>Anticoagulation for PE</u><br><br>* Consider <u>thrombolysis for PE</u> if high risk for decompensation (e.g., severe RV dysfunction) or deterioration despite anticoagulation.<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Consider a temporary <u>IVC filter</u>.<br><br>* Consider <u>embolectomy for PE</u> in patients at high risk of decompensation.<br><br><br> |
| <u>Massive PE</u> | <br><br>* <u>Thrombolysis for PE</u> followed by anticoagulation.<br><br>* <u>Embolectomy for PE</u> if <u>thrombolysis</u> fails.<br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Embolectomy for PE</u><br><br> |





### Unstable patients




#### Management of massive PE [[22]](/library/Z_YZ57)[[48]](/library/qV1Cvf0)[[54]](/library/q11C3f0)




* <u>Hypoxemic respiratory failure</u>: Optimize oxygenation (e.g., using <u>HFNC</u>) and consider <u>mechanical ventilation</u>.

* <u>Hemodynamic instability</u>

* Consider ≤ 500 mL IV fluid bolus.

* Avoid <u>volume overload</u>.

* Begin <u>vasopressor</u> or <u>inotrope</u> infusion if the patient remains hypotensive, e.g., <u>norepinephrine</u> DOSAGE or <u>dobutamine</u>. DOSAGE [[22]](/library/Z_YZ57)

* Consider temporary <u>mechanical circulatory support</u>.

* Urgent reperfusion

* Begin <u>thrombolysis for PE</u> immediately if there are no absolute <u>contraindications to thrombolytics for massive PE</u>.

* If <u>thrombolysis</u> is contraindicated or fails: Consult interventional radiology or <u>surgery</u> to perform <u>embolectomy for PE</u>. [[48]](/library/qV1Cvf0)





> [!WARNING]
> Avoid <u>volume overload</u> during resuscitation. Aggressive fluid administration can worsen impaired RV function and further decrease <u>cardiac output</u>. [[22]](/library/Z_YZ57)




#### Management of cardiac arrest due to PE [[56]](/library/HnXKuA)[[57]](/library/ogV0wF0)




* Start <u>ACLS</u>   [[56]](/library/HnXKuA)

* Consider <u>POCUS</u> to identify indirect <u>signs of PE</u>.  [[56]](/library/HnXKuA)[[58]](/library/Rr1lSR0)[[59]](/library/ir1JSR0)[[60]](/library/LgVwDF0)

* Subxiphoid view (consider only during <u>pulse</u> check): thin-walled (< 5 mm), dilated RV

* Lower extremity views: <u>US findings of DVT</u>

* Consider intra-arrest <u>thrombolytics</u> (e.g., <u>tPA</u> DOSAGE).  [[56]](/library/HnXKuA)[[61]](/library/3r1SSR0)

* Consider  <u>ECLS</u> (e.g, <u>VA-ECMO</u>). [[5]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[48]](/library/qV1Cvf0)





![Dilated right heart with right ventricular strain](media/hn6egd9yxdgwk9i23y393bbq.jpg)

Dilated right heart with right ventricular strain

![POCUS protocol for detection of lower extremity DVT](media/ibhxrbtm6tkih2tuu4cauvm1.jpg)

POCUS protocol for detection of lower extremity DVT

![Ultrasound of deep vein thrombosis (DVT)](media/t7s1nvbrjts85rz7j9kiq9rd.jpg)

Ultrasound of deep vein thrombosis (DVT)




### Stable patients [[22]](/library/Z_YZ57)[[25]](/library/9XXNZC)[[54]](/library/q11C3f0)




* Symptomatic <u>nonmassive PE</u> and low-risk <u>submassive PE</u>: Prescribe <u>anticoagulation for PE</u> if bleeding risk is low.

* High-risk <u>submassive PE</u>: Start <u>anticoagulation for PE</u> and consider <u>thrombolysis for PE</u>.

* Incidentally discovered <u>PE</u> : Treat the same as symptomatic <u>PE</u>.

* Subsegmental <u>PE</u> : Consider surveillance after ruling out <u>proximal DVT</u> if the risk of recurrence is low.

* <u>Recurrent VTE</u>: Consider starting <u>low molecular weight heparin</u> if a <u>direct oral anticoagulant</u> or <u>vitamin K antagonist</u> was being used prior to recurrence.  [[25]](/library/9XXNZC)[[62]](/library/_KY5QJ)[[63]](/library/8P1OgS0)





### Disposition [[20]](/library/xsdECr0)[[22]](/library/Z_YZ57)[[25]](/library/9XXNZC)[[54]](/library/q11C3f0)




<u>PESI</u> and <u>sPESI score</u> can be used to help guide disposition.




* Low-risk <u>PE</u> (<u>PESI</u> class I–II or <u>sPESI score</u> = 0)

* Consider outpatient management in consultation with specialists.

* Unless contraindicated, begin <u>anticoagulation for PE</u> before discharge and arrange close follow-up.

* Criteria for outpatient management include:

* Hemodynamic stability and adequate room air oxygenation

* <u>Opiates</u> are not required for <u>pain</u> relief.

* Availability of family or social support, easy <u>access to health care</u>

* No other major comorbidities or reasons for hospitalization

* Intermediate-risk <u>PE</u> or high-risk <u>PE</u> (<u>PESI</u> class ≥ III or <u>sPESI score</u> ≥ 1)

* Hospitalization is required; consult <u>PERT</u> if available.

* <u>ICU</u> admission: commonly necessary for <u>massive PE</u> or patients with severe RV dysfunction [[5]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

---

## Anticoagulation

### Bleeding risk assessment [[25]](/library/9XXNZC)[[54]](/library/q11C3f0)[[64]](/library/2_YTn7)




Evaluate a patient's risk for <u>major bleeding</u> and identify contraindications before initiating anticoagulation. [[48]](/library/qV1Cvf0)




* See “<u>Risk of major bleeding on anticoagulant therapy in patients with VTE</u>.”   [[65]](/library/xdbEHs)[[66]](/library/Xe19xf0)

* <u>Contraindications to anticoagulation</u> include : [[67]](/library/EP18gS0)[[68]](/library/be1Hxf0)

* Significant active bleeding

* Recent high-risk bleeding (e.g., intracranial)

* Recent major <u>surgery</u>

* Severe <u>thrombocytopenia</u>





> [!TIP]
> The benefits of anticoagulation in <u>PE</u> outweigh the bleeding risks in most patients who do not have an absolute <u>contraindication to anticoagulation</u>. [[68]](/library/be1Hxf0)




![HAS-BLED score: Bleeding risk in atrial fibrillation](media/rlvuqhrcp6rg4x3otcjwx6ot.jpg)

HAS-BLED score: Bleeding risk in atrial fibrillation




### Empiric anticoagulation for PE [[22]](/library/Z_YZ57)[[25]](/library/9XXNZC)[[54]](/library/q11C3f0)[[64]](/library/2_YTn7)




Empiric anticoagulation may be started while waiting for a definitive diagnosis, depending on the risk of bleeding, the <u>PTP of PE</u>, and the expected timing of the diagnostic study.




* Indications

* <u>High PTP of PE</u>: Initiate in all patients.

* <u>Intermediate PTP of PE</u>: Consider in all patients.

* <u>Low PTP of PE</u>: only if imaging is expected to be delayed for > 24 hours

* Contraindication: <u>risk of major bleeding on anticoagulant therapy in patients with VTE</u>

* Choice of medication

* Stable patients: <u>low molecular weight heparin</u> (<u>LMWH</u>)  DOSAGE  [[64]](/library/2_YTn7)

* Unstable patients or patients with <u>renal insufficiency</u>: <u>unfractionated heparin</u> (<u>UFH</u>) DOSAGE [[62]](/library/_KY5QJ)





### Initial anticoagulation (first 5–10 days) [[25]](/library/9XXNZC)[[54]](/library/q11C3f0)[[62]](/library/_KY5QJ)[[69]](/library/T_Y6n7)




The selection of the initial <u>anticoagulant</u> depends on the severity of the <u>PE</u>, patient comorbidities, and/or planned concurrent treatment. [[48]](/library/qV1Cvf0)




* <u>LMWH</u> (e.g., <u>enoxaparin</u> DOSAGE) or <u>fondaparinux</u> DOSAGE ;  [[64]](/library/2_YTn7)[[70]](/library/U_Ybn7)

* Preferred over <u>UFH</u> in most patients with normal renal function  [[22]](/library/Z_YZ57)

* <u>Anticoagulant</u> of choice for <u>PE</u> in pregnant patients [[22]](/library/Z_YZ57)

* <u>LMWH</u> is recommended over <u>UFH</u> for patients with cancer. [[71]](/library/rk1f6S0)

* <u>UFH</u> DOSAGE ;  [[48]](/library/qV1Cvf0)[[69]](/library/T_Y6n7)

* Preferred in patients with <u>renal failure</u>

* Preferred if <u>thrombolysis</u>, embolectomy, or <u>mechanical circulatory support</u> are planned

* Preferred in patients with unpredictable subcutaneous absorption (e.g., patients with <u>obesity</u>, <u>hypoperfusion</u>)

* Initial oral anticoagulation

* Consider as initial therapy for low-risk <u>PE</u>.

* Agents: <u>rivaroxaban</u> DOSAGE or <u>apixaban</u> DOSAGE





### Long-term anticoagulation (up to 3 months) [[25]](/library/9XXNZC)[[54]](/library/q11C3f0)[[69]](/library/T_Y6n7)




* <u>Direct oral anticoagulant</u> (<u>DOAC</u>)

* Preferred over <u>vitamin K antagonist</u> (<u>VKA</u>) for most patients

* No initial <u>parenteral anticoagulation</u> is required with <u>rivaroxaban</u> DOSAGE or <u>apixaban</u> DOSAGE

* Initial <u>parenteral anticoagulation</u> is required with <u>dabigatran</u> DOSAGE or <u>edoxaban</u> DOSAGE

* <u>VKA</u>: <u>warfarin</u> DOSAGE

* Therapeutic target: <u>INR</u> 2–3 [[64]](/library/2_YTn7)

* Preferred over <u>LMWH</u> when a <u>DOAC</u> cannot be used [[69]](/library/T_Y6n7)

* Long-term <u>parenteral anticoagulation</u> with <u>LMWH</u>

* Preferred over <u>VKA</u> in patients with cancer if a <u>DOAC</u> cannot be used [[71]](/library/rk1f6S0)

* Preferred in pregnant patients [[62]](/library/_KY5QJ)





#### Extended anticoagulation (> 3 months) [[25]](/library/9XXNZC)[[54]](/library/q11C3f0)[[62]](/library/_KY5QJ)




* Reassess the need for anticoagulation after 3 months, then annually.

* Indications for extended anticoagulation

* <u>Unprovoked PE</u> with a low to moderate risk of bleeding

* <u>Provoked PE</u> secondary to a chronic <u>risk factor</u> with a low to moderate risk of bleeding

* Patients with <u>active cancer</u> with any level of bleeding risk [[71]](/library/rk1f6S0)

---

## Reperfusion therapy

### Bleeding risk assessment [[48]](/library/qV1Cvf0)




Evaluate a patient's risk for <u>major bleeding</u> and identify contraindications before initiating <u>thrombolytics</u>.




* Identify <u>risk factors for bleeding in patients with VTE</u>.

* Evaluate absolute vs. relative <u>contraindications to thrombolysis for PE</u>.

* Carefully consider the risk-benefit <u>ratio</u> of therapy.

* Consider the following interventions to reduce bleeding risk: [[68]](/library/be1Hxf0)

* Optimize <u>antihypertensive therapy</u>.

* Stop or minimize the use of <u>antiplatelet medications</u> and <u>NSAIDs</u>.

* Correct reversible renal and/or hepatic disease.

* Treat potential bleeding sources.





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Thrombolysis for PE</u> is associated with a high risk of <u>major bleeding</u>.




### Thrombolysis for PE [[25]](/library/9XXNZC)[[48]](/library/qV1Cvf0)




Follow local protocols in consultation with a <u>thrombosis</u> specialist.




#### Systemic <u>thrombolysis</u> [[54]](/library/q11C3f0)[[62]](/library/_KY5QJ)




* Procedure: administration of <u>thrombolytic therapy</u> through a peripheral <u>vein</u>

* Indications

* <u>Massive PE</u> (<u>hemodynamic instability</u> and/or <u>right heart failure</u>) with a low bleeding risk

* <u>Nonmassive PE</u> with a low bleeding risk, if patients deteriorate despite anticoagulation

* <u>Cardiac arrest</u> in patients with suspected <u>PE</u>

* Contraindications: See “<u>Contraindications to thrombolysis for PE</u>.”

* Common thrombolytic agents  [[5]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[22]](/library/Z_YZ57)[[72]](/library/KAcUkU0)

* <u>Recombinant tissue plasminogen activator</u> (<u>tPA</u>), e.g., <u>alteplase</u> (preferred) DOSAGE

* <u>Streptokinase</u>

* <u>Urokinase</u>

* Management of anticoagulation [[73]](/library/WSbPAG)

* Discontinue anticoagulation prior to <u>thrombolysis</u>.

* Check <u>aPTT</u> 2 hours after completion of <u>thrombolysis</u>.

* Resume anticoagulation when <u>aPTT</u> is < 2 times the <u>upper limit of normal</u>.

* Complication: hemorrhage during thrombolytic treatment  [[74]](/library/iSbJzG)





#### <u>Catheter-directed thrombolysis</u> [[75]](/library/2k1TMS0)




* Procedure

* Direct infusion of <u>thrombolytics</u> into the obstructed <u>pulmonary artery</u> via pulmonary <u>arterial catheter</u>

* May be combined with mechanical or <u>ultrasound</u> fragmentation of the <u>embolus</u>

* Indication: Alternative to systemic <u>thrombolysis</u> in patients with a high bleeding risk.

* Contraindications: See “<u>Contraindications to thrombolysis for PE</u>.”





#### Contraindications




| <br>Contraindications to thrombolysis for pulmonary embolism  [[22]](/library/Z_YZ57)[[48]](/library/qV1Cvf0)[[62]](/library/_KY5QJ)<br> |  |
| --- | --- |
| <u>Absolute contraindications</u> | <br><br>* Active bleeding<br><br>* Prior <u>intracranial hemorrhage</u><br><br>* <u>Ischemic stroke</u> ≤ 3 months ago<br><br>* Recent spinal or <u>brain</u> <u>surgery</u><br><br>* Structural intracranial disease<br><br>* Recent <u>head trauma</u> with <u>brain injury</u> or <u>fracture</u><br><br>* <u>Bleeding diathesis</u><br><br><br> |
| <u>Relative contraindications</u> | <br><br>* Uncontrolled <u>hypertension</u><br><br>* Current anticoagulation use<br><br>* Recent nonintracranial bleeding<br><br>* Recent <u>surgery</u>, invasive procedure, or trauma<br><br>* <u>Ischemic stroke</u> > 3 months ago<br><br>* Traumatic <u>CPR</u><br><br>* <u>Pregnancy</u><br><br>* Age > 75 years<br><br>* Weight < 60 kg<br><br>* <u>Pericardial</u> fluid or <u>pericarditis</u><br><br>* <u>Diabetic retinopathy</u><br><br><br> |





### Embolectomy for PE [[48]](/library/qV1Cvf0)




* Indications

* <u>Contraindications to thrombolysis for PE</u> in patients with <u>massive PE</u> or high-risk <u>submassive PE</u>

* Failure of <u>thrombolysis for PE</u>

* Options

* Surgical embolectomy: removal of the <u>embolus</u> through an <u>incision</u> in the <u>pulmonary artery</u>

* <u>Endovascular embolectomy</u>: catheter-based <u>thrombus</u> removal [[75]](/library/2k1TMS0)

---

## Complications

* High risk of recurrence: Without <u>anticoagulant</u> treatment, the risk of recurrence is ∼ 10% in the first year and ∼ 5% per year after.  [[21]](/library/-xYD_r)

* <u>Right ventricular failure</u> and secondary <u>pulmonary arterial hypertension</u>

* <u>Sudden cardiac death</u> due to <u>pulseless electrical activity</u>

* <u>Atelectasis</u> (∼ 20% of cases)

* <u>Pleural effusion</u>

* Pulmonary infarction (∼ 10% of cases)

* Embolisms of smaller segmental <u>arteries</u> can lead to wedge-shaped hemorrhagic <u>pulmonary infarctions</u>.

* <u>Right ventricular failure</u>, increased bronchial venous pressure, and preexisting pulmonary diseases increase the risk.

* Patients may present with <u>pneumonia</u> following <u>pulmonary infarction</u>, detected by peripheral infiltration on <u>chest x-ray</u> (typically wedge-shaped = <u>Hampton's hump</u>).

* <u>Arrhythmia</u>





![Pulmonary embolism with infarction from pneumonia (left side)](media/f8opywl3keo14shu6gq8mfpd.jpg)

Pulmonary embolism with infarction from pneumonia (left side)




We list the most important complications. The selection is not exhaustive.

---
